unit.title: Install electrical and electronic apparatus, machinery, fixtures and secondary wiring

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before you install new equipment, what should you check against the drawings and specification?
options: That the right items and ratings were delivered
That the boxes are the same colour as the last order
That the delivery came before ten in the morning
That the driver signed his name on the delivery van

questions.stem: A new light fitting is delivered with a cracked cover. What should you do?
options: Fit it, and fill the crack with silicone later
Fit it, as the crack will not affect the light
Do not fit it; report it and get a replacement
Fit it in a dark corner where nobody will see

questions.stem: Why should you look at the site before fixing equipment to a wall?
options: To decide which colour paint the wall will need later
To check the wall material, access and hidden services
To count the windows and doors for the client's records
To see whether the room is cool enough to work in

questions.stem: Before using a power drill, what should you check?
options: That it is the newest drill in the Centre's store
That the chuck key is taped to the drill's lead
That the drill is the heaviest one you can find
That the lead, plug and body are not damaged

questions.stem: Where should you look for the mounting height and position of a fixture?
options: On the price list from the electrical supplier
In a phone photo from a different building
In the drawings and the specification
On the label of the fixture's cardboard box

questions.stem: Before you connect new equipment to an existing circuit, what must be done?
options: Isolate, lock off, tag and prove the circuit dead
Switch the circuit off at the switch on the wall
Ask someone to keep an eye on the breaker board
Work fast, using one hand, while the circuit is on

questions.stem: What PPE is needed when drilling into a concrete block ceiling above your head?
options: Ear defenders only, as drilling is loud
Rubber gloves only, to protect your hands
A cap only, to keep dust out of your hair
Safety glasses and a dust mask, at least

questions.stem: A 40 kg motor must be lifted onto its base. What is the safest way?
options: One person lifts it quickly, bending over at the waist
Plan the lift and use a hoist or a proper team lift
Roll it up a plank while standing in front of it
Drag it up onto the base by its terminal box

questions.stem: Why should the area under a ladder or work platform be kept clear and coned off?
options: So the floor can be swept while you work above
So the ladder can be moved by someone else
So nobody is hit by a dropped tool or part
So the client can see that work is being done

questions.stem: When fixing a light fitting from a ladder, which is safe practice?
options: Keep three points of contact and do not overreach
Stand on the top step to get closer to the ceiling
Lean the ladder on the light fitting for support
Lean out to the side so you need not move the ladder

questions.stem: You must fix a heavy panel to a hollow concrete block wall. How should the fixings be chosen?
options: Use the smallest screws, so the blocks do not crack
Use whatever fixings are left over from the last job
Use nails, as they go in faster than screws
Use fixings rated for the load and that type of wall

questions.stem: Why should you drill the hole size stated by the fixing maker?
options: So the drill bit lasts much longer before it gets blunt
So the fixing grips tightly and holds its full load
So the hole can be filled more easily later on
So less dust is made while drilling the hole

questions.stem: A panel will be fixed where a pump makes it shake. What should be used on its fixings?
options: Lock washers or self-locking nuts
Extra grease put on every thread
Plastic tape wrapped round each bolt
Shorter bolts with no washers

questions.stem: Why must a ceiling fan be fixed to a box or support rated for a fan?
options: So the fan blades turn in the right direction
So the fan uses less electricity when it runs
Its weight and shaking can pull a lamp box out
So the fan's speed control switch works smoothly

questions.stem: How should a heavy light fitting be supported?
options: By its own supply cable, as the cable is strong
By tape around the cable and the fitting
By resting it on the ceiling boards only
By its own fixings to the building structure

questions.stem: Why should you check for hidden cables and pipes before drilling a wall?
options: So the drill does not slip and mark the paint
Drilling into them can cause a shock or a leak
So the hole can be drilled in a straight line
So the client knows where to hang pictures later

questions.stem: How can you check that a motor pulley and the driven pulley are in line?
options: Look along the belt from the far end of the workshop
Run the motor and listen to the sound of the belt
Lay a straight edge across the faces of both pulleys
Measure the length of the belt with a tape

questions.stem: What happens if a drive belt is fitted much too tight?
options: The motor and pulley bearings wear out early
The belt slips and squeals every time it starts
The motor runs faster than its rated speed
The belt lasts longer because it cannot move

questions.stem: Before a motor is coupled to its load, an authorised person runs it on its own for a moment. Why?
options: To polish the shaft before the coupling goes on
To warm the motor's windings up, ready for the load
To use up the grease that is in the bearings
To check that it turns in the right direction

questions.stem: What must be fitted over a belt drive before the machine is run?
options: A sheet of cardboard taped over the belt and pulley
A fixed guard that covers the belts and pulleys
A warning sign, as long as no one goes near it
A cloth over the pulleys to keep the dust off

questions.stem: Why are the bolts holding a motor to its base tightened evenly, and checked again after a short run?
options: To keep it aligned and stop it working loose
To make the motor run at a higher speed than before
To let the motor move about as it warms up
To make the motor easier to remove later

questions.stem: Why must a metal-bodied (Class I) light fitting be connected to the protective earth?
options: So that the lamp gives out more light when it is on
So that the fitting stays cool when it is in use
So a fault to the metal body trips the protection
So that the switch works more quietly

questions.stem: Which light fitting should be chosen for an outdoor wall that gets rain?
options: Any indoor fitting, as long as it is a strong one
One with an IP rating suited to outdoor use
The cheapest fitting that the supplier has in stock
One with a clear glass cover so more light gets out

questions.stem: When fitting a luminaire, why must the cable entry be sealed and the gasket fitted?
options: To make the luminaire heavier and more solid
To stop the lamp from turning in its holder
To make the luminaire easier to take down
To keep out dust, water and insects

questions.stem: In a control panel, what is usually meant by 'secondary wiring'?
options: The control and signal wiring between devices
The main incoming supply cable from the street
The earth rod and its cable outside the building
The spare wiring kept in the store for repairs

questions.stem: Why is each control wire in a panel fitted with a numbered marker?
options: So the wire is easier to cut to the right length
So that the panel looks neater when the door is open
So it matches the diagram and can be traced later
So the wire can carry a bigger current safely

questions.stem: How much insulation should be stripped from a conductor for a screw terminal?
options: As much as possible, so that the joint is strong
About 50 mm, so the wire can be wrapped round
None at all, as the screw will cut through the insulation
Just enough for the terminal, with no bare wire showing

questions.stem: Why must there be no loose strands sticking out of a terminal?
options: They make the terminal hard to undo later
A stray strand can touch the next terminal
They make the wire look untidy to the client
They stop the wire marker from fitting on

questions.stem: Why must the crimp tool and its die match the crimp terminal being fitted?
options: So the tool lasts longer and does not need oiling
So the terminal is the same colour as the tool
So the crimp is tight and will not pull off
So the terminal can be fitted with one hand only

questions.stem: After crimping a terminal onto a wire, how should you check it?
options: Look at the crimp and give the wire a firm pull
Tap the terminal with a hammer to settle it in
Heat the crimp with a lighter flame to soften it
Bend the wire back and forth a few times

questions.stem: Why should power cables and low-voltage signal cables be kept apart in a panel?
options: So that the panel door shuts more easily
So that the power cables stay cooler
So that each cable type can be a different colour
So noise from power cables does not upset signals

questions.stem: Why must a cable not be bent tighter than the maker's minimum bending radius?
options: It makes the cable harder to label later
It can damage the insulation and the cores
It makes the cable able to carry less voltage
It changes the colour of the outer sheath

questions.stem: How do you choose the right size of cable gland?
options: Match it to the outside diameter of the cable
Use the largest gland so the cable fits easily
Match it to the size of the enclosure's lid
Use the size printed on the light bulb

questions.stem: When a metal gland is used on a steel-wire armoured cable, what else does the gland usually do?
options: It lets the cable carry a higher current
It cools the cable where it enters the box
It stops the cores from being colour-coded
It connects the armour to earth

questions.stem: After the cables are glanded, why must the enclosure lid and its seal be fitted correctly?
options: So that the lid can be opened without tools
So that the box looks the same as the others
So that the enclosure keeps its IP rating
So that the cables inside can move about freely

questions.stem: When handling a circuit board, why should you wear an anti-static wrist strap connected to an earth point?
options: To keep your hands clean while you work on it
To stop static from your body damaging the parts
To protect you from the mains supply voltage
To hold the board steady on the bench while you work

questions.stem: How should a circuit board be held?
options: By its edges, without touching the parts or tracks
By the largest part on it, as it is the strongest
With a firm grip right across the middle of the board
By its connecting wires, so it hangs freely

questions.stem: Why must electronic equipment be disconnected before an insulation resistance test?
options: So that the test finishes more quickly
So the reading is shown in amps
So the equipment can cool down
The high test voltage can damage it

questions.stem: Which test checks that the protective earth conductor is joined all the way to each metal part?
options: Insulation resistance test
Functional test
Earth continuity test
Motor speed test

questions.stem: What does a very low insulation resistance reading between line and earth usually show?
options: The insulation is in very good condition indeed
The insulation is damaged or there is a fault
The tester's battery is now fully charged up
The circuit is ready to be switched on

questions.stem: Who should switch on the supply to newly installed equipment for the first time?
options: The first trainee who finishes their own part of the task
The client, so that they can see it working
Anyone, as long as the cover has been fitted
An authorised person, after the dead tests pass

questions.stem: Why are the dead tests done before the supply is switched on?
options: To find faults safely before the circuit is live
To use up the time before the inspector arrives
To warm the cables up before the load is added
To show the client that the test meter is working

questions.stem: What is a functional test?
options: Checking the cable sizes against the price list
Measuring the resistance of the earth rod
Checking that the controls work as planned
Counting the number of screws used in the job

questions.stem: What should be handed over with the finished installation?
options: The leftover cable, the tools and the empty boxes
Test results, marked-up drawings and the manuals
A list of the trainees' phone numbers and names
The receipts for the workers' lunch and travel

questions.stem: What should you do with cable offcuts and packaging at the end of the job?
options: Leave them in the ceiling space out of sight
Push them inside the panel for later use
Burn them behind the workshop to save time
Clear them up and dispose of them correctly

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What width, in millimetres, is the common 'top hat' DIN rail used in control panels?
What is the name of the small metal tube crimped onto fine stranded wire before it goes into a screw terminal?
What do the letters ESD stand for?
A leaning ladder is set 1 m out from the wall for every how many metres of height?
What tool, with a bubble in a small glass tube, is used to check that a fixture is level or upright?
Insulation resistance is usually read in a large unit of resistance. What is this unit called?
What is the name of the plug used to seal an unused entry hole in an enclosure?
To reverse a three-phase motor, with the supply isolated, how many of the supply phase connections are swapped over?
What are the thin metal packing pieces put under motor feet to level and align the motor called?
What is the name of the plastic channel with a clip-on lid that carries wiring neatly inside a panel?
What is the name of the plastic fixing pushed into a drilled hole in concrete block, so that a screw can grip?
What do the letters PLC stand for?
Which test checks that a switch is connected in the line conductor and not in the neutral?
What tool is used to cut a clean, round hole in a metal enclosure for a cable gland?
What is the name of the crimp terminal with a round hole, used to connect a conductor to a stud or bolt?

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and prepare to install a small control panel on a workshop wall.
essays.modelAnswer: I study the drawings, the wiring diagram and the specification to find the panel's position, mounting height, the parts in it and how it is wired. I check the materials delivered against the parts list: the enclosure, DIN rail, breakers, contactor, overload relay, terminals, push buttons, lamps, glands, cable and wire markers, and I check that the ratings match the drawings. I look at the site: the wall material (often hollow concrete block), access, the clear space in front of the panel, and any hidden cables or pipes. I choose fixings rated for the panel's weight and for the wall. I collect and check the tools and test instruments: drill and bits, crimp tool, screwdrivers, an approved voltage tester and an insulation resistance tester, all in good condition and in date. I plan the safe isolation of any supply I must connect to: switch off, lock off, tag and prove dead with a tester checked before and after use. I agree the work with the supervisor, and plan the PPE, barriers and clean-up.
markingPoints: Studies the drawings, wiring diagram and specification
Checks the materials and their ratings against the parts list and drawings
Surveys the site (wall material, access, clear space, hidden services) and chooses rated fixings
Collects and checks tools and test instruments
Plans safe isolation, PPE and barriers, and agrees the work with the supervisor

essays.stem: Describe how to mount an enclosure or a heavy fixture securely on a hollow concrete block wall.
essays.modelAnswer: First I mark the position and height from the drawing, and use a spirit level to mark level and upright lines. I check the wall with a cable and pipe detector so that I do not drill into hidden services, and I wear safety glasses and a dust mask. I hold the enclosure in place, or use its template, to mark the fixing holes. I choose fixings that are made for hollow block and rated for the weight, as the fixing maker says. I drill the exact size and depth stated, with a masonry bit, keeping the drill square to the wall. I clean the dust out of the holes and fit the fixings. Then I fix the enclosure with the right screws and washers, check it again with the level, and tighten the screws evenly without cracking the case. Finally I push firmly on the enclosure to check that it is secure, and clean up the dust and offcuts.
markingPoints: Marks the position from the drawing and uses a spirit level
Checks for hidden services and wears PPE
Chooses fixings made for hollow block and rated for the weight
Drills the stated size and depth, cleans the holes and fits the fixings
Fixes, re-levels, tightens evenly, checks it is secure and cleans up

essays.stem: Explain how to terminate stranded control conductors correctly in a control panel.
essays.modelAnswer: I cut each conductor to the right length, so it reaches its terminal neatly without being tight or leaving a big loop. I slide on the wire marker with the number from the wiring diagram before I terminate. I strip only the length of insulation the terminal needs, using the correct stripper so that the strands are not nicked or cut. For fine stranded wire going into a screw terminal, I crimp on a bootlace ferrule of the right size with the matching crimp tool, so no strand can escape. For a stud, I use a ring terminal crimped with the correct die. I give each crimp a firm pull test. I put the conductor fully into the terminal, with no bare copper showing outside and no insulation under the screw, and tighten it to the torque the maker gives, using a torque screwdriver. Then I check that there are no stray strands, that each wire goes to the terminal shown on the diagram, and that the wiring lies tidily in the trunking.
markingPoints: Cuts to length and fits the correct wire marker from the diagram
Strips the right length without damaging the strands
Fits a ferrule or ring terminal with the matching crimp tool, and pull-tests it
Inserts fully with no bare copper showing and tightens to the maker's torque
Checks for stray strands, checks against the diagram, and leaves the wiring tidy

essays.stem: Explain how to install a motor on its base and line it up with the machine it drives by a belt, including the safety checks.
essays.modelAnswer: The supply to the motor is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead before I start. I lift the motor with a hoist or a planned team lift. I place it on the base and fit the bolts loosely. If the base is uneven, I put shims under the feet so that all four feet sit firmly. I fit the pulleys, then lay a straight edge across the faces of the motor pulley and the driven pulley to check that they are in line, and move the motor until they are. I tighten the base bolts evenly and check the alignment again. I connect the supply through its local isolator, with the earth connected, and do the dead tests. An authorised person checks the direction of rotation with the belt off. After isolating again, I fit the belt and set its tension as the maker says: not too tight, which wears the bearings, and not too loose, which makes it slip. The belt guard is fitted before the machine is run, and after a short run the bolts and belt tension are checked again.
markingPoints: Safe isolation of the supply and a safe lift
Bolts fitted loosely, feet shimmed so all sit firmly
Pulleys lined up with a straight edge; bolts tightened evenly and re-checked
Earth connected, dead tests done, direction checked by an authorised person with the belt off
Belt tension set as the maker says; guard fitted before running; checked again after a short run

essays.stem: Explain why power cables and signal or data cables are kept apart, and describe how to run secondary wiring neatly and safely in a panel.
essays.modelAnswer: Power cables carry large currents that make electrical 'noise'. If signal or data cables run close beside them, this noise can get into the signals and cause false readings or faults in controllers and sensors. So power and signal cables are kept apart, in separate trunking or with a gap between them, and if they must cross, they cross at a right angle. Screened signal cables are used where needed, with the screen earthed as the drawing says, usually at one end. Circuits of different voltages are kept separate as the drawing and the code require. In the panel, I run the control wiring in trunking, not loose, without overfilling it, so the lid fits and heat can escape. Wires go in neat runs, with bends no tighter than the maker allows, and each one has a marker at both ends. Wires to the door are bundled in a loop that lets the door open without strain. Cable ties are snug but not crushing.
markingPoints: Noise from power cables can upset signals and cause faults
Keep them apart (separate trunking or a gap), and cross at right angles
Screened cables earthed as the drawing says; different voltage circuits kept separate
Wiring in trunking that is not overfilled, with proper bends and markers at both ends
Door loop allows movement; ties snug but not crushing

essays.stem: Describe the dead tests carried out on a new installation before it is switched on, and say why each test is done.
essays.modelAnswer: Dead tests are done with the circuit isolated, locked off and proved dead, so that faults are found safely before the supply is connected. First I do a continuity test of the protective (earth) conductors, to check that every metal part and earth terminal is joined back to the main earth, so that a fault will trip the protection. Then I test the continuity of the circuit conductors, to check that there are no breaks in the line and neutral conductors. Next I do an insulation resistance test between the live conductors, and between the live conductors and earth, after disconnecting electronic equipment that the test voltage could damage. A low reading shows damaged insulation or a fault. Then I do a polarity test, to check that switches and protective devices are in the line conductor and that equipment is connected the right way round. I compare each result with the values the code or specification gives, and record them. Only when all tests pass does an authorised person switch on for the live checks and functional tests.
markingPoints: Done isolated and proved dead, to find faults safely before switching on
Protective conductor (earth) continuity, and why
Continuity of the circuit conductors, and why
Insulation resistance, with electronics disconnected, and what a low reading means
Polarity; results compared and recorded; an authorised person switches on only when all pass

essays.stem: Explain how electronic apparatus, such as a controller, a sensor or a circuit board, should be protected during installation.
essays.modelAnswer: Electronic parts can be damaged by static electricity from my body, which I may not even feel. Before handling a circuit board, I wear an anti-static wrist strap connected to an earth point, work on an anti-static mat if there is one, and keep the board in its anti-static bag until it is fitted. I hold boards by their edges and do not touch the parts, pins or tracks. I check the supply voltage and type (AC or DC) against the nameplate, and connect DC supplies the right way round, because a reversed connection can destroy the device. I keep signal cables away from power cables and earth the screens as the drawing says, to avoid noise. I fit the device in a clean, dry enclosure with the right IP rating, away from heat, dust and water. Before an insulation resistance test I disconnect electronic devices, as the high test voltage can damage them. I follow the maker's instructions for mounting, cooling space and connections.
markingPoints: Static protection: wrist strap to earth, mat, anti-static bags
Boards held by the edges without touching parts or tracks
Correct supply checked; DC connected the right way round
Signal cables kept from power cables; suitable clean, dry enclosure
Electronics disconnected before insulation tests; maker's instructions followed

essays.stem: Explain how to choose and fit cable glands so that an enclosure keeps its IP rating.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check the enclosure's IP rating and the location, such as indoors, outdoors or a wash-down area, and choose glands with at least the same IP rating. I measure the outside diameter of each cable and choose a gland whose clamping range suits that size. I also choose the right type for the cable, such as a plain plastic gland for a PVC-sheathed cable, or a metal gland with an armour clamp for steel-wire armoured cable. I make the entry hole the correct size with a hole saw or punch, remove the sharp edges, and fit the gland with its sealing washer and locknut, tightened firmly. I pass the cable through, strip the sheath inside the enclosure only, and tighten the gland's seal onto the cable sheath so it grips without crushing. Where an armoured cable is used, the armour is clamped and connected to earth. Any unused entry holes are closed with blanking plugs. Finally the lid and its seal are fitted correctly.
markingPoints: Glands with at least the enclosure's IP rating, suited to the location
Gland sized to the cable's outside diameter and of the right type
Correct hole size, sharp edges removed, sealing washer and locknut fitted
Seal tightened on the sheath without crushing; armour clamped and earthed
Unused holes blanked and the lid and seal fitted correctly

essays.stem: Describe how newly installed equipment is commissioned and handed over to the client.
essays.modelAnswer: Commissioning starts only when the installation is complete and all the dead tests have passed and been recorded. I check that all covers, guards and labels are fitted, that the area is clean, and that everyone has been told the equipment is about to be switched on. An authorised person then switches on the supply and carries out the live checks the code requires, such as testing that RCDs trip correctly. Then the functional tests are done: switches, push buttons, lamps, controls and safety devices such as emergency stops are checked, and motors are checked for the right direction and for unusual noise, heat or vibration. If a fault is found, the equipment is switched off, isolated and put right before testing again. I record the results on the test sheet. Then I hand over to the client: I show them how to use the equipment safely, and give them the test results, the marked-up drawings, and the makers' manuals and warranty papers, and I get their signature.
markingPoints: Starts only after all dead tests have passed and been recorded
Covers, guards and labels fitted; area clean; people told
An authorised person switches on and does the required live checks
Functional tests of controls and safety devices; motors checked; faults isolated and put right
Results recorded; client shown how to use it and given test results, drawings and manuals

essays.stem: Describe how to work safely at height when fixing light fittings to a ceiling.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check whether the job can be done from a work platform or a mobile tower, which is safer than a ladder for longer jobs. If a ladder or step ladder is used, I check it before use for broken rungs, damaged feet and loose parts, and make sure it is tall enough so that I do not stand on the top steps. A leaning ladder is set at about 1 out for every 4 up, on firm, level ground, and tied or footed by another person. I keep three points of contact, keep my body between the stiles and never overreach; I move the ladder instead. I carry tools in a belt or pass them up in a bag, so my hands are free. The area below is coned off so that nobody walks underneath. The circuit is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead before I touch the wiring. Heavy fittings are lifted with help, and a ladder is never used close to overhead lines.
markingPoints: Chooses a platform or tower where possible; inspects the ladder before use
Sets the ladder up correctly: about 1 out for 4 up, firm level ground, tied or footed
Three points of contact, no overreaching, tools carried safely
Area below coned off
Circuit isolated and proved dead before touching wiring; help with heavy fittings

practical1.title: Mount and wire a small motor control panel (secondary wiring)
practical1.brief: As a group, mount and wire a small control panel on the training wall or a wiring board, from the drawing and wiring diagram the assessor gives. The panel holds a DIN rail with a control circuit breaker, a contactor, an overload relay and terminal blocks, and has a start push button, a stop push button and a 'running' lamp on its door or front. The group: (1) checks the parts against the parts list and the ratings against the drawing; (2) marks out, drills and fixes the enclosure level and secure; (3) fixes the DIN rail and mounts the devices; (4) wires the control circuit with stranded conductors, ferrules and numbered wire markers, run neatly in trunking; (5) glands the incoming supply cable and the motor cable with suitable glands, and blanks any unused holes; (6) carries out the dead tests (continuity of the protective conductor, continuity of each control wire against the diagram, and insulation resistance) and records them. The group does NOT connect the panel to any supply. When all the tests pass, the instructor connects and energises it, and the group watches the functional test (start, hold in, stop, overload trip). Share the work so that every member mounts at least one device, wires at least three conductors and does at least one test while the assessor watches. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Small enclosure with a door, a DIN rail and wiring trunking
Control circuit breaker, contactor with an auxiliary contact, overload relay and terminal blocks
Start and stop push buttons and a 'running' indicator lamp
Stranded control wire, bootlace ferrules, ring terminals and numbered wire markers
Cable glands to suit the cables, and blanking plugs
Fixings rated for the wall, a drill and masonry bits, and a hole saw or punch
Screwdrivers, torque screwdriver, wire strippers and a ratchet crimp tool
Spirit level, tape measure, and a cable and pipe detector
Continuity tester, insulation resistance tester and a test record sheet
Drawing, wiring diagram and parts list from the assessor
Safety glasses, dust masks and safety boots
photos: The parts laid out and checked against the parts list
The enclosure fixed to the wall, with the spirit level on top
The DIN rail and devices mounted, before wiring
Close-up of terminations: ferrules fitted, markers on, no bare copper showing
The finished wiring in the trunking, with the lid off
The glands fitted and unused holes blanked
The dead tests being done, and the completed test record
The functional test by the instructor, with the 'running' lamp lit
checklist: Checked the parts and their ratings against the drawing and parts list
Checked for hidden services, wore PPE, and fixed the enclosure level and secure with suitable fixings
Mounted the devices firmly on the DIN rail where the drawing shows
Stripped, ferruled and terminated conductors correctly, tightened to the maker's torque, with no stray strands
Fitted wire markers that match the wiring diagram at both ends of each wire
Ran the wiring neatly in trunking with suitable bends, keeping power and control wiring apart
Chose and fitted glands to suit the cables, and blanked unused holes
Carried out and recorded the dead tests correctly
Did not connect any supply, and left energising to the instructor
safety: The group never connects the panel to a supply; only the instructor energises it, after the dead tests pass
Any supply point used is isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after use
Check for hidden cables and pipes before drilling; wear safety glasses and a dust mask
Clamp the work when using a hole saw or punch, and remove sharp edges from holes
Keep the work area tidy and offcuts off the floor
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Mount, align and connect a small motor with a belt drive, a local isolator and a light fitting
practical2.brief: As a group, install a small motor (single-phase or three-phase, as the Centre has) on a base or training frame so that it drives a pulley or a small load by a V-belt, with a lockable local isolator, and a light fitting over the work position. The group: (1) checks the motor nameplate against the supply and the drawing; (2) lifts the motor onto the base safely (a hoist or a planned team lift) and fits the bolts loosely; (3) shims the feet if needed, lines up the pulleys with a straight edge, tightens the bolts evenly and checks the alignment again; (4) fixes the isolator and the light fitting and runs the cables in conduit or trunking with suitable glands; (5) connects the motor, isolator and light fitting, with every earth connected; (6) does the dead tests and records them. The instructor then energises the circuit and checks the direction of rotation with the belt off, and then isolates, locks off and proves dead again. The group then (7) fits the belt, sets its tension as the maker says, re-checks the alignment and fits the belt guard. Finally the instructor runs the machine while the group stands clear and checks for noise, heat and vibration. Every member takes part in the lift, the alignment, at least one termination and at least one test while the assessor watches. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A small motor with a pulley, and a base or training frame with a driven pulley or small load
V-belt and belt guard
Shims, bolts, nuts and lock washers
A lockable local isolator, a light fitting and its switch
Cable, conduit or trunking, glands and fixings
Straight edge, spirit level, spanners and screwdrivers
Continuity tester, insulation resistance tester and a test record sheet
A hoist, or lifting help as the Centre's rules require
Safety glasses, safety boots and gloves
photos: The motor nameplate, and the supply details on the drawing
The motor being lifted onto the base safely
The straight edge across both pulleys, showing them in line
The isolator, light fitting and cable runs fixed in place
The motor terminal box connected, with the earth connected
The dead tests being done, and the completed test record
The belt fitted, the tension checked and the guard in place
The test run, with the area clear
checklist: Checked the motor nameplate against the supply and the drawing
Lifted the motor safely, using a hoist or a planned team lift
Levelled the motor with shims and lined up the pulleys with a straight edge
Tightened the bolts evenly and set the belt tension as the maker says
Fixed the isolator and light fitting securely and ran the cables neatly with suitable glands
Made correct, tight terminations with every earth connected
Carried out and recorded the dead tests correctly
Fitted the belt guard before the machine was run
Stood clear during the direction check and test run, and left energising to the instructor
safety: The group never energises the circuit; only the instructor switches on, after the dead tests pass
Before the belt is fitted or touched, the instructor isolates, locks off, tags and proves dead with a tester checked before and after use
Never run the machine with the belt on and the guard off; keep hands, hair and clothing clear of belts and pulleys
Lift heavy motors with a hoist or a planned team lift, keeping your back straight
Wear safety glasses and safety boots throughout
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
